newsitem.title: UK: OPEC set for output freeze at talks next week.
newsitem.headline: OPEC set for output freeze at talks next week.

text.p: Little more than a week ahead of their biannual talks, OPEC ministers showed no sign on Monday they planned to boost output to take advantage of a prolonged oil price rally and increased demand for their oil.

Given the usual uncertainties over winter demand and the timing of the implementation of a long-delayed Iraqi oil sale deal, the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) probably will maintain the current 25.03 million barrel per day ceiling until June 1997, OPEC delegates said.
"Don't rock the boat should be our motto at this meeting," said a delegate from an OPEC Gulf member.
OPEC sources said not one of the 11 OPEC members is expected to push for an increase in the ceiling when the group meets in Vienna on November 27.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, is not keen to open up old wounds by discussing who should get what part of any ceiling increase. And Iran, OPEC's second largest producer, is not convinced the market could absorb more OPEC oil at this time, sources said.
"No one has a good reason for changing anything right now. We are enjoying the desserts of the oil price rally," one OPEC official said.

By resisting the temptation to raise individual quotas, something the group has not done since September 1993, analysts said OPEC should keep intact a rally which has sent oil prices soaring to their highest levels in nearly six years.

"(A rollover) implies continued OPEC production 'creep' rather than a surge in early 1997, which in turn would indicate a fairly well-blanced if not slightly tight market for several months to come," veteran OPEC watcher Mehdi Varzi of Kleinwort Benson said.
In a recent report, Varzi and other Kleinwort oil analysts said they expected to increase their 1997 price forecasts for world benchmark North Sea crude oil Brent.
Ahead of the OPEC meeting, Kleinwort said it expected Brent to average $20 a barrel in the first half of 1997 compared with $23.10 on Monday.
"We expect to offer a new higher forecast once the outcome of the OPEC meeting is announced," Kleinwort said in its report.

OPEC and other oil producers are enjoying the benefits of windfall oil revenues as Middle East tension, very low oil inventories and surging demand have pushed oil prices far above even the most optimistic forecasts.
The OPEC reference basket price hit $22.65 on Friday and has averaged nearly $20 so far in 1996, well above the $16.86 1995 average.
Analysts reckon OPEC should earn an extra $25 billion in oil revenue this year which may have made members complacent about dealing with quota violations.

Nearly all 11 OPEC members are producing more than their individual allotments, pushing collective output to 26 million bpd for the first time since 1980, when OPEC had two more members. That does not even include the full 1.2 million bpd assigned to Iraq since a much-delayed UN oil-for-food deal has yet to be implemented.

With the notable exception of influential Gulf OPEC members Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, most of the world's oil producers inside and outside OPEC are pumping as much oil as they can which leaves the world susceptible to supply shocks.

"There is little slack left in the supply chain outside of OPEC and prices have to take most of the strain as the market lurches from one short-term crisis to the next," a report from the Centre for Global Energy Studies said on Monday.
Since oil stocks, especially in the key consumer markets of the United States and Europe, are so low ahead of the peak winter demand period, the market will remain volatile for months, traders said.
"The oil market has no effective buffer against unexpected variations in demand and supply," the CGES said.
